title: Building the Neuromuscular Junction: Agrin, Lrp4 and MuSK

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What three structural features mark a chemical synapse such as the neuromuscular junction?
cards.back: Transmitter vesicles in the presynaptic terminal, a narrow cleft, and a thickened postsynaptic membrane containing concentrated receptors and their supporting proteins.
cards.quote: a narrow cleft between the two cells, and a thickened postsynaptic membrane, where receptors and the proteins that hold them are concentrated.
cards.section: The sorting problem

cards.front: Why is the neuromuscular junction a useful model for studying synapse formation?
cards.back: It is large, accessible outside the brain, and comparatively simple: acetylcholine is its transmitter and the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is its major receptor.
cards.quote: It is large, it lies outside the brain where you can reach it, and it is simple: one transmitter, acetylcholine, and one major receptor,
cards.section: The sorting problem

cards.front: At the skeletal neuromuscular junction, the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a {{c1::ligand-gated}} channel.
cards.back: Acetylcholine binding opens the channel and lets cations into the muscle.
cards.quote: a channel that opens when acetylcholine binds and lets cations into the muscle.
cards.section: The sorting problem

cards.front: What is the basal lamina surrounding a skeletal muscle fibre?
cards.back: A thin layer of extracellular matrix that wraps the fibre and also lies in the neuromuscular junction cleft.
cards.quote: The NMJ cleft also holds a sheet of basal lamina, the thin layer of extracellular matrix that wraps each muscle fibre.
cards.section: The sorting problem

cards.front: At a mature neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine receptors are concentrated {{c1::under the nerve ending}}.
cards.back: They are sparse elsewhere on the muscle fibre.
cards.quote: At a mature junction the receptors are packed under the nerve ending and sparse everywhere else on the fibre.
cards.section: The sorting problem

cards.front: How do muscle and nerve divide the work of organizing postsynaptic receptor clusters in developing mouse skeletal muscle?
cards.back: Muscle builds initial clusters without a nerve. The nerve supplies agrin to protect selected clusters and acetylcholine to disperse unprotected ones.
cards.quote: The muscle builds receptor clusters with its own machinery, and needs no nerve to do it. The nerve decides which clusters stay.
cards.section: The sorting problem

cards.front: Regenerated frog muscle clusters receptors at old synaptic sites on surviving basal lamina even when nerves are excluded. What does this show?
cards.back: The surviving extracellular matrix retains information locating the old synaptic sites; a newly arriving nerve is not required to mark those sites again.
cards.quote: regenerating muscle fibres clustered receptors at the old sites even with the nerve kept out.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: How can a single gene produce protein forms with different activities in nerve and muscle?
cards.back: Alternative splicing cuts and joins the gene's RNA in different ways, producing different protein forms.
cards.quote: The difference is splicing, in which one gene's RNA is cut and joined in more than one way.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: The muscle-surface receptor that binds neural agrin is {{c1::Lrp4}}.
cards.back: Lrp4 also forms a complex with MuSK.
cards.quote: In 2008 two laboratories showed that Lrp4 is the agrin receptor.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: How does MuSK activation use the general receptor tyrosine kinase mechanism?
cards.back: Two kinase domains are brought together and phosphorylate each other, enabling signaling.
cards.why: Mice lacking MuSK make no junctions, showing that this muscle signaling component is essential.
cards.quote: MuSK signals when two kinase domains are brought together and phosphorylate each other
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: A ligand binds muscle cells but not an isolated signaling kinase. How could expressing a candidate surface protein in nonmuscle cells test its role in ligand recognition?
cards.back: Compare ligand binding in cells with and without the candidate. Acquired binding supports a role in recognition; it does not alone establish direct binding between purified proteins.
cards.quote: One test: give the candidate to cells that are not muscle and ask whether they now bind agrin.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: Nonmuscle cells gain neural-agrin binding after receiving Lrp4. What further evidence distinguishes direct Lrp4 binding from binding mediated by another cell protein, and connects it to MuSK?
cards.back: Test purified proteins: neural agrin binds purified Lrp4, and Lrp4 binds MuSK. The rule is that cell-based binding supports receptor function, whereas purified-protein binding establishes the direct interactions in the relay.
cards.quote: purified neural agrin binds purified Lrp4, and that Lrp4 also binds MuSK.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: What does Dok7 do in developing mouse muscle, and what happens without it?
cards.back: Dok7 is an intracellular adaptor that binds phosphorylated MuSK and boosts its activity. Mice lacking Dok7 make no neuromuscular junctions.
cards.quote: Dok7, an adaptor inside the muscle, binds phosphorylated MuSK and boosts its activity. Mice lacking Dok7 make no junctions, so that boost is not optional.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: Trace the signaling relay from nerve-derived agrin to clustered muscle acetylcholine receptors.
cards.back: Neural agrin → Lrp4 → MuSK with Dok7 → rapsyn → clustered acetylcholine receptors.
cards.quote: neural agrin → Lrp4 → MuSK (with Dok7) → rapsyn → clustered AChR
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: A developing mouse makes neural agrin but lacks muscle Lrp4. Should agrin preserve normal neuromuscular junction formation, and why?
cards.back: No. Lrp4-deficient mice have defects resembling MuSK mutants: supplying the signal cannot replace its missing muscle-surface receptor.
cards.quote: Mice lacking Lrp4 were reported in 2006 to have NMJ defects resembling those of MuSK mutants.
cards.section: How the nerve's signal was found

cards.front: What is the muscle prepattern in the embryonic mouse diaphragm?
cards.back: A central band of acetylcholine receptor clusters, with receptor-subunit RNA concentrated in the same region, laid down without motor innervation.
cards.quote: The muscle had laid down a prepattern: a rough map of where the junctions would go, drawn without the nerve.
cards.section: The muscle starts without the nerve

cards.front: Two hypotheses say either motor axons or muscle place the first receptor clusters. What observation in a mouse diaphragm never reached by motor axons favors muscle placement?
cards.back: A central band of receptor clusters still forms. Because motor axons never arrived, the band cannot require prior positioning by those axons.
cards.quote: The diaphragm still built a band of receptor clusters across its middle, the region where the nerve would normally have arrived.
cards.section: The muscle starts without the nerve

cards.front: Why does a receptor cluster on an uninnervated muscle cell not establish that a neuromuscular synapse has formed?
cards.back: A cluster is a postsynaptic feature. Without a nerve terminal, it has no presynaptic partner; receptor clustering alone does not constitute a synapse.
cards.quote: Contact makes far more clustering and narrows the band, and without a nerve the clusters belong to no terminal.
cards.section: The muscle starts without the nerve

cards.front: The enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine is {{c1::choline acetyltransferase (ChAT)}}.
cards.back: Motor neurons lacking ChAT release no acetylcholine.
cards.quote: Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) is the enzyme that makes acetylcholine, so motor neurons in mice lacking ChAT release none.
cards.section: A paradox, and a second force

cards.front: Why can agrin-deficient mouse muscle form early receptor clusters yet retain markedly fewer and smaller clusters later?
cards.back: The muscle starts clusters without agrin, but acetylcholine disperses clusters lacking agrin protection, so most early clusters are lost.
cards.quote: Acetylcholine, released at every terminal, disperses receptor clusters that agrin does not protect. Without agrin, little protects them, so most are lost.
cards.section: A paradox, and a second force

cards.front: A developing mouse lacks ChAT but retains agrin. Compared with normal muscle, what happens to receptor-cluster abundance and band width, and why?
cards.back: More clusters persist over a wider band. Agrin protection remains while loss of acetylcholine removes the main dispersing force; nerve branching also widens.
cards.quote: With the main dispersing force gone, the muscle keeps more clusters, spread over a wider band, and the nerve branches widely.
cards.section: A paradox, and a second force

cards.front: ChAT is deleted in an agrin-deficient mouse with intact muscle clustering machinery. What happens to receptor clusters, and why?
cards.back: Clusters return despite the absence of agrin. Removing acetylcholine removes the dispersing force, allowing the muscle's MuSK-dependent program to retain clusters.
cards.quote: Instead, clusters return, built by the muscle's own MuSK-dependent program.
cards.section: A paradox, and a second force

cards.front: Agrin deletion causes cluster loss, but deleting both agrin and ChAT restores clusters in developing mouse muscle. Why does this distinguish an obligatory cluster inducer from a protective signal?
cards.back: An obligatory inducer could not be bypassed just by removing acetylcholine. Rescue therefore supports protection against dispersal as a major agrin function. The rule combines muscle-autonomous cluster formation with opposing nerve signals; it does not exclude agrin-induced clustering.
cards.quote: If agrin were required to make clusters, removing acetylcholine could not bring them back.
cards.section: A paradox, and a second force

cards.front: In the working model of developing mouse muscle, why do receptor clusters beneath terminals survive despite receiving acetylcholine?
cards.back: Agrin anchored in synaptic basal lamina provides strong local protection. Under the terminal, this protection outweighs dispersal; distant clusters usually lack that protection.
cards.quote: agrin is anchored in the synaptic basal lamina, so its protection stays under the terminal, while the dispersing effect of acetylcholine reaches clusters elsewhere on the fibre.
cards.section: Why the cluster under the terminal survives

cards.front: A transmitter knockout widens both a muscle receptor-cluster band and nerve branching. Does this prove the transmitter normally acts directly on distant clusters? Explain the limitation.
cards.back: No. The rule is that changing two spatial features together does not isolate the route of action. Wider nerve branching accompanies the wider cluster band, so this result alone does not establish how a dispersing signal reaches distant clusters.
cards.quote: though these mice also have wider nerve branching. How the dispersing signal reaches distant clusters is not settled.
cards.section: Why the cluster under the terminal survives

cards.front: Why is a strict agrin-on/agrin-off switch inadequate to explain the few small clusters in agrin-null mouse muscle?
cards.back: Without agrin, MuSK is thought to retain lower activity driven by Lrp4. Some clusters can therefore survive; a strict switch would predict none.
cards.quote: Without agrin, MuSK is thought to keep a lower level of activity, driven by Lrp4, so a few small clusters are kept.
cards.section: Where the two forces meet

cards.front: Neural agrin is delivered to a nonsynaptic site on an innervated adult rodent muscle fibre. What local postsynaptic outcome is expected, and why?
cards.back: A new postsynaptic specialization can form there. Agrin is instructive: local delivery can organize a specialization, consistent with MuSK signaling both initiating and protecting clusters.
cards.quote: In adult rodent muscle, neural agrin delivered to non-synaptic sites of innervated fibres induces new postsynaptic specializations there
cards.section: Where the two forces meet

cards.front: High muscle MuSK expression permits mouse synapses to form without agrin. Does this show that acetylcholine disperses clusters by reducing MuSK signaling?
cards.back: No. The balance rule permits either reduced MuSK signaling or a separate dispersal pathway resisted by strong MuSK signaling. Bypass by extra MuSK shows signaling strength can compensate, but does not distinguish those mechanisms.
cards.quote: Whether acetylcholine works by turning MuSK signaling down, or by a separate route that strong MuSK signaling can resist, is not settled.
cards.section: Where the two forces meet

cards.front: How does nerve-driven activity restrict acetylcholine receptor gene expression along a multinucleated muscle fibre?
cards.back: It suppresses receptor transcription in nuclei away from the synapse, while nuclei beneath the terminal continue transcribing receptor genes.
cards.quote: When the nerve drives the fibre, receptor transcription is suppressed in nuclei away from the synapse, while the few nuclei beneath the terminal keep transcribing receptor genes,
cards.section: A second effect of activity: the nuclei

cards.front: After denervation, how should a muscle fibre respond to acetylcholine applied far from its old junction, and why?
cards.back: It becomes more sensitive. Removing nerve activity lifts suppression of receptor-gene transcription away from the junction, allowing receptors to appear along the fibre.
cards.quote: Cut the nerve and the suppression lifts: receptors appear along the whole fibre, and the denervated muscle becomes "supersensitive" to acetylcholine applied anywhere on it.
cards.section: A second effect of activity: the nuclei

cards.front: How do receptor-cluster dispersal and suppression of receptor-gene transcription differ?
cards.back: Dispersal removes existing clusters. Transcriptional suppression reduces production of receptors away from the synapse.
cards.quote: Dispersal removes clusters that already exist. Suppressed transcription means fewer receptors are made away from the synapse.
cards.section: A second effect of activity: the nuclei

cards.front: In rapsyn-null mouse muscle, subsynaptic nuclei still transcribe receptor genes although receptors do not cluster. What proposed dependency does this refute?
cards.back: It refutes the idea that local receptor-gene transcription requires assembled receptor clusters. Rapsyn-dependent clustering and subsynaptic transcription can be separated.
cards.quote: The rapsyn-null mouse separates clustering from local transcription: no clusters, yet subsynaptic nuclei keep transcribing.
cards.section: A second effect of activity: the nuclei

cards.front: A model says muscle only receives organizing signals from the nerve. How do MuSK/Lrp4-mutant mouse phenotypes and muscle Lrp4 signaling challenge it?
cards.back: Axons wander and terminals fail to differentiate without MuSK or Lrp4; muscle Lrp4 also signals back to the nerve. The rule is reciprocal specialization: the muscle signaling complex helps organize both sides, rather than merely receiving nerve instructions.
cards.quote: In mouse work, muscle Lrp4 also signals back to the nerve terminal, so the same complex helps organize the presynaptic side.
cards.section: Signals in both directions

cards.front: What synapse-building principle transfers from the neuromuscular junction to central synapses despite their different molecular organization?
cards.back: Both partners send signals that make the other specialize, and stable synapses require both sides.
cards.quote: What carries over is the logic: each partner sends signals that make the other specialize, and stable synapses need both sides.
cards.section: NMJ vs. central synapses, and a junction that fails

cards.front: What causes myasthenia gravis, and which neuromuscular-junction protein is the antibody target in most patients?
cards.back: The immune system makes antibodies against the junction; most patients have antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor. Muscles tire and weaken with use.
cards.quote: In myasthenia gravis, the immune system makes antibodies against the junction, and muscles tire and weaken with use. Most patients have antibodies against the AChR.
cards.section: NMJ vs. central synapses, and a junction that fails

cards.front: An autoimmune process targets a muscle's acetylcholine receptors while leaving its motor axon present. Would axon contact alone guarantee normal junction function, and why?
cards.back: No. Muscle weakness can occur despite the axon's presence, because the postsynaptic receptor is also needed. Stable synapses require specialization on both sides.
cards.quote: Most patients have antibodies against the AChR.
cards.section: NMJ vs. central synapses, and a junction that fails

cards.front: Predict receptor clustering in a developing mouse lacking both MuSK and ChAT. What would finding clusters imply?
cards.back: No clusters are predicted. The rule combines MuSK-dependent construction with acetylcholine-driven dispersal: removing dispersal cannot rescue absent construction. Clusters would imply a MuSK-independent construction route. This is a prediction, not a reported double-mutant result.
cards.quote: Removing acetylcholine lets clusters survive only if the muscle can make them, and without MuSK it cannot.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Two normally innervated mouse lines express extra MuSK across each muscle fibre. Only the higher-expression line develops clusters outside the normal band. How does the balance rule explain this?
cards.back: Only the higher dose supplies enough MuSK signaling to resist dispersal away from terminals. Extra MuSK need not alter the pattern unless its signaling crosses that functional threshold.
cards.quote: A small increase might change nothing, so the prediction needs a dose.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why is adhesion between an axon and muscle insufficient evidence that a postsynaptic specialization has formed?
cards.back: Adhesion holds the cells together. Building a postsynaptic specialization requires additional organization; physical contact alone does not demonstrate it.
cards.quote: Adhesion holds the partners together. It does not by itself make a postsynaptic specialization.
cards.section: The first contact

cards.front: A motor axon contacts cultured muscle between its existing spontaneous receptor clusters. Must it move to an old cluster for strong clustering to follow? Why?
cards.back: No. In culture the axon does not seek out pre-existing clusters; much greater clustering follows where it contacts the muscle.
cards.quote: it does not seek out those clusters, but where it touches, far more clustering follows.
cards.section: What the axon does in a dish

cards.front: Surface muscle acetylcholine receptors are labeled red before adding motor neurons. Later, green labels only newly surfaced receptors. Contact clusters contain 1,200 red and 800 green receptors. What percentage was already on the surface before neuron addition?
cards.back: Old-surface fraction = red/(red + green) = 1,200/(1,200 + 800) = 0.60 = 60%. Both previously surface-exposed and newly surfaced receptors contribute to clusters.
cards.quote: it does not seek out those clusters, but where it touches, far more clustering follows.
cards.section: What the axon does in a dish
